title: Salt (Mark 9:42–50)
hook: have salt in yourselves, and be at peace with one another

segments.voice: Yesterday, John tried to stop a stranger, and heard forbid him not. Your line was not against us, for us. Whose good work did you notice? Day one hundred ninety-nine.

Still in the same house, still talking to the friends who argued about rank, Jesus says some of the hardest-sounding things in Mark. Whoever trips up one of these little ones who believe, it would be better for them to have a millstone hung around their neck and be thrown into the sea. If your hand makes you stumble, cut it off. If your foot, cut it off. If your eye, pluck it out. Better to enter life missing a part than be thrown whole into Gehenna, the valley outside Jerusalem that became a picture of ruin. These sayings are meant to land like a slap. Most Christians have always read them as deliberate exaggeration, not instructions. And then, right at the end, the tone changes, and he talks about something on every kitchen table.
screen: `A MILLSTONE AND THE SEA.` → `CUT IT OFF.` → `SOMETHING ON EVERY TABLE.`

segments.voice: In the King James Bible: "Salt is good: but if the salt have lost his saltness, wherewith will ye season it? Have salt in yourselves, and have peace one with another." Salt was precious. It kept fish and meat from rotting before refrigerators. It gave taste. In the Hebrew Bible, offerings were seasoned with salt, and there's a phrase, a covenant of salt, for a promise meant to last. Can salt really lose its saltness? Pure salt can't. But much of the salt people used then was gathered from the Dead Sea region, mixed with other minerals. Many explain that damp could wash the true salt out, leaving white stuff that looked like salt and tasted of nothing. Right before this, there's a line nobody is sure about: everyone will be salted with fire. Scholars have puzzled over it for centuries, and Mark doesn't explain it. What is clear is the ending. Have salt in yourselves, and peace with one another. Remember who he's talking to: the men who argued about who's greatest, and shut out the stranger. Keep your taste, your bite, your faith. And then don't use it on each other. That closes this stretch of Mark, the one that kept asking who is this. Washed hands and what comes out of the heart. Crumbs for a mother's daughter. Be opened. Seven baskets. Hard hearts in a boat. Men like trees. You are the Christ. Take up your cross. Listen to him. Help my unbelief. Who's the greatest. Not one of us. And salt. Tomorrow the road turns south, toward Jerusalem.
screen: `SALT KEPT THINGS AND GAVE TASTE.` · `SALT THAT LOSES ITS SALTNESS.` · `SALTED WITH FIRE: NOBODY'S SURE.` · `SALT IN YOU, PEACE WITH EACH OTHER.` · then, large: `HAVE SALT IN YOURSELVES, AND HAVE PEACE ONE WITH ANOTHER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: make peace with one person. Settle, and breathe. Think of someone you're a little crossways with right now. Not the biggest wound of your life; something smaller. A sharp text. A cold week. A silence that went on too long. Picture them. Keep your salt: you don't have to pretend you were wrong about everything. But ask what one step toward peace would look like. A message. A kind word. Letting it go. If you pray, you can bring them to God by name. The bell holds the time.
Salt. It keeps things and gives them taste. Have salt in yourselves, he says, and have peace one with another.
Your line: salt, and peace. Today, take the one step toward peace you chose, and keep your flavor while you do it. Day one hundred ninety-nine.

howItsDone: Christians often speak of being "the salt of the earth" and read Mark 9:50 as a call to keep their faith lively and to make peace within the church; many congregations share the peace, a greeting or handshake, during worship.

fork.setup: you're one of the twelve. you've argued about rank and shut out a stranger. what's his last word to you in this passage?
options: guard the group and keep it pure.
have salt in yourselves, and have peace one with another.
the greatest will be salted with fire.
fork.reveal: keep your salt, and have peace with each other. said to the very men who'd been arguing.

original.note: Greek: salt. Mark 9:50 uses it three times in one verse.

trapdoor: what you thought: salt is just a thing to shake on fries.
what it means: keep your taste and your faith alive, and don't use it on one another: salt, and peace.
what a scholar hears: offerings seasoned with salt and a covenant of salt in the Hebrew Bible; salted with fire in 9:49 remains a puzzle.

notes: Gehenna described as 'the valley outside Jerusalem that became a picture of ruin' (Valley of Hinnom); confirm.
The explanation of salt 'losing its saltness' (impure Dead Sea salt leached by damp) is a common but not certain explanation; attributed to 'many'. Confirm.
